plan: Literary narrative (CLD-P-ACT-R-000057), an original story: a fourteen-year-old helps a departing neighbor plant tulip bulbs he will not see bloom, watches them come up for the new family, and chooses not to put the reason into words. Narrator's gender unstated; items use 'the narrator'. No bulb or tulip passage in the ACT Reading bank. Ten questions, four aimed at hard (unstated motive, inferred emotion, function of a detail, closing sentence). Plus R056-02 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-R-000056 (choice D replaced). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Bulbs
passages.text:
Mr. Halvorsen had sold his house in August, and he was moving to his daughter's apartment across the state on the first of November. So I did not understand why, on a gray afternoon in late October, he asked me to help him plant two hundred tulip bulbs along the front walk.

"They won't come up until April," I said, kneeling beside him with the trowel. I was fourteen and believed that pointing out the obvious was a kind of help.

"That's right," he said, and handed me another bulb. He showed me how deep to set each one—three times its own height—and which end to point toward the sky. His hands, which had built half the fences on our street, shook a little now, so he let me dig while he sorted the bulbs by color in his lap: red ones near the steps, yellow ones by the mailbox, a few white ones scattered where, he said, they would surprise people.

We worked until the light went thin. I kept waiting for him to explain, and he kept not explaining. Once he stopped and looked at the house for a long time, and I looked at the dirt, because that seemed like the polite thing to do.

The family who bought the house moved in the week after he left. They had a little boy who rode a red tricycle up and down the walk all winter, over the place where the bulbs were sleeping. I watched from my window and said nothing to anyone.

In April the tulips came up exactly as he had arranged them, red by the steps and yellow by the mailbox. The white ones appeared in odd places, one beside the drain spout, two under the maple, and the boy's mother stood in the yard one morning with her coffee, turning slowly, as if someone had left her a message she was still working out how to read.

I wrote to Mr. Halvorsen that week. I told him about the colors and the white ones under the maple. I did not ask him why he had planted them. By then I thought I knew, and I suspected that if I wrote the reason down, it would come out smaller than it was.

passages.title: Written in Light
passages.text:
On a summer evening in a meadow, the flashes of fireflies can look random, a scattering of sparks with no pattern at all. To the fireflies themselves, they are anything but. In many species, the flashes are a conversation between potential mates, and each species has its own dialect.

In a typical exchange, a male flies over the grass flashing a pattern specific to his species: a single long flash, perhaps, or a quick double pulse repeated every few seconds. A female of the same species, perched on a leaf below, answers after a precise delay. The timing of her reply matters as much as the flash itself. A male who sees a flash at the wrong interval is likely to keep flying, because the reply does not come from a female of his kind. When the timing is right, he lands and approaches, and the two may exchange flashes several more times before they meet.

Because the code is so specific, it can be exploited. Females of one group of fireflies, known as Photuris, are able to imitate the replies of females from other species. A male of another species who sees the right response at the right delay flies down expecting a mate and instead finds a predator. The Photuris female eats him. She gains more than a meal: the males she catches carry defensive chemicals that make fireflies distasteful to spiders and birds, and Photuris females, which cannot make these chemicals themselves, take them in from their prey.

Researchers have found that some Photuris females adjust their imitation to whatever species of male is flying nearby, switching from one reply pattern to another during a single evening. This flexibility has led some biologists to describe the females as aggressive mimics. Others prefer more cautious language, noting that the switching may be less a matter of deliberate choice than of a simple rule: answer whatever flash pattern appears overhead.

For the males being imitated, the risk creates a kind of arms race. A male who approaches every reply quickly may find mates sooner, but he is also more likely to be eaten. In some populations, males of preyed-upon species approach answering females more slowly and flash more times before landing, as if testing the reply. The meadow's apparent randomness, in other words, conceals not only courtship but also deception, appetite, and caution, all written in light.

candidates.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the passage?

choices.A: A teenager helps a departing neighbor plant bulbs and later grasps why.
choices.B: A teenager convinces an elderly neighbor not to sell his house and move away.
choices.C: A new family discovers that the previous owner left the garden in poor condition.
choices.D: An elderly man teaches a teenager to build fences along their shared street.

candidates.evidence: By then I thought I knew
candidates.explanation: The narrator helps plant bulbs without understanding why, sees them bloom for the new family, and by the end believes they understand the gesture.

B.rationale: Mr. Halvorsen has already sold the house and moves as planned.

C.rationale: The new family finds tulips blooming, not a neglected garden.

D.rationale: Fences are mentioned only as part of his past; they plant bulbs together.

hints: How does the narrator's understanding change?

strategy.explanation: Compare the first and last paragraphs.

candidates.remember: A summary of a narrative should capture its change, not just its events.

candidates.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that Mr. Halvorsen planted the bulbs mainly in order to:

choices.A: increase the price he could get when he sold the house to a new family.
choices.B: teach the narrator a skill that would be useful for a future job.
choices.C: leave a pleasant surprise for whoever would live there after him.
choices.D: make sure the tulips would bloom before he moved away on November first.

candidates.evidence: a few white ones scattered where, he said, they would surprise people
candidates.explanation: He planted knowing he would be gone before they bloomed, arranged them carefully, and placed some "where they would surprise people," so the gift was for whoever came after.

A.rationale: He had already sold the house in August.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests the planting was about the narrator's job prospects.

D.rationale: The narrator points out the tulips won't come up until April, and he agrees.

hints: When would the tulips bloom, and where would he be?

strategy.explanation: Combine the timing with his comment about surprising people.

candidates.remember: When a character's action benefits only others, that is often its point.

author_checklist.hardness: The motive is never stated and must be inferred from timing and the placement of the white bulbs.

candidates.stem: The narrator's description of pointing out the obvious as "a kind of help" mainly serves to:

choices.A: criticize Mr. Halvorsen for failing to explain his plans clearly.
choices.B: show, in hindsight, the narrator's youthful lack of understanding.
choices.C: suggest that the narrator was rude to Mr. Halvorsen that afternoon.
choices.D: explain why the narrator later decided to become a gardener.

candidates.evidence: I was fourteen and believed that pointing out the obvious was a kind of help.
candidates.explanation: The older narrator looks back with gentle irony on the fourteen-year-old who thought stating the obvious was useful.

A.rationale: The remark is about the narrator, not a criticism of Mr. Halvorsen.

C.rationale: The narrator is naive, not rude; Mr. Halvorsen simply agrees.

hints: Who is commenting on the fourteen-year-old?

strategy.explanation: Notice the narrator looking back on a younger self.

candidates.remember: "I was fourteen and believed" signals an older narrator's hindsight.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Mr. Halvorsen told the narrator to set each bulb:

choices.A: so that the red ones were nearest the mailbox.
choices.B: with the pointed end facing toward the ground.
choices.C: in a single straight line along the walk.
choices.D: at a depth three times its own height.

candidates.explanation: The third paragraph says he showed the narrator to set each bulb three times its own height deep.

A.rationale: The red ones went near the steps.

B.rationale: He showed which end to point toward the sky.

hints: Find the dash in the third paragraph.
candidates.remember: Distractors in detail questions often swap details from nearby sentences.

candidates.stem: When Mr. Halvorsen "looked at the house for a long time," the narrator looks at the dirt most likely because the narrator:

choices.A: senses he feels something private and does not want to intrude.
choices.B: is bored with the work and wants to finish before dark.
choices.C: disapproves of Mr. Halvorsen's decision to sell the house.
choices.D: needs to concentrate on setting the bulbs at the correct depth.

candidates.evidence: I looked at the dirt, because that seemed like the polite thing to do
candidates.explanation: Looking away "seemed like the polite thing to do," which suggests the narrator senses Mr. Halvorsen's emotion and gives him privacy.

B.rationale: The narrator stays until the light goes and says looking away seemed polite.

D.rationale: The narrator says looking away "seemed like the polite thing to do."

hints: What reason does the narrator give for looking at the dirt?

strategy.explanation: Read the end of the fourth paragraph.

candidates.remember: Characters' small gestures often reveal what they sense but do not say.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must infer the emotion the narrator senses from a stated reason about politeness.

candidates.stem: The detail that the boy rode his tricycle "over the place where the bulbs were sleeping" mainly serves to:

choices.A: suggest that the boy damaged many of the bulbs before they could bloom.
choices.B: show that the narrator disliked the new family that moved into the house.
choices.C: emphasize that the gift was hidden and unknown to the new family all winter.
choices.D: explain why some of the white tulips appeared in unexpected places.

candidates.evidence: over the place where the bulbs were sleeping
candidates.explanation: The boy rides over the bulbs without knowing they are there, which stresses the hidden gift that only the narrator knows about until spring.

A.rationale: The tulips came up "exactly as he had arranged them."

B.rationale: The narrator watches silently; no dislike is expressed.

D.rationale: Mr. Halvorsen scattered the white ones on purpose.

hints: What does the family not know during the winter?

strategy.explanation: Connect the detail to the narrator's silence.

candidates.remember: A detail's function often lies in what one character knows and another does not.

author_checklist.hardness: A tempting distractor reads the detail literally as damage, which the passage contradicts.

candidates.stem: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word thin most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: Light that "went thin" was fading in the late afternoon, so "thin" means "faint."

A.rationale: Light is not described as having width.

C.rationale: This describes a body or object, not light.

D.rationale: Light cannot be diluted with water.

hints: What happens to daylight late on an October afternoon?

strategy.explanation: Predict from the time of day.

candidates.remember: Pick the meaning that fits what the word describes.

candidates.stem: The description of the boy's mother "turning slowly, as if someone had left her a message" suggests that she:

choices.A: senses the flowers were planted on purpose for someone to find.
choices.B: is searching the yard for the boy's lost tricycle.
choices.C: is reading a letter that Mr. Halvorsen sent to her.
choices.D: disapproves of the colors that the flowers turned out to be.

candidates.evidence: as if someone had left her a message she was still working out how to read
candidates.explanation: The comparison to a message she is working out how to read suggests she senses intention behind the arrangement of the flowers.

B.rationale: She is looking at the flowers, not searching for anything.

C.rationale: The "message" is a comparison; no letter is mentioned.

hints: What does "as if" tell you about the message?

strategy.explanation: Treat the message as a comparison.

candidates.remember: "As if" introduces a comparison, not a literal event.

candidates.stem: In the last sentence, the narrator suggests that writing down the reason for the planting would have:

choices.A: embarrassed Mr. Halvorsen in front of his daughter.
choices.B: revealed that the narrator had guessed the reason wrong.
choices.C: proved to Mr. Halvorsen that the narrator had been paying attention.
choices.D: made the gesture seem smaller than it was.

candidates.evidence: it would come out smaller than it was
candidates.explanation: The narrator fears that putting the reason into words "would come out smaller than it was," that is, explaining the gesture would diminish it.

A.rationale: No embarrassment or daughter's reaction is suggested.

B.rationale: The narrator believes the guess is right; the concern is about putting it into words.

C.rationale: The narrator chooses not to write the reason, so nothing is proved.

hints: What does "come out smaller" refer to?
candidates.remember: Closing sentences often explain a character's choice not to speak.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must interpret a figurative concern about language diminishing meaning.

candidates.stem: The passage is narrated from the point of view of:

choices.A: Mr. Halvorsen, explaining why he decided to plant the bulbs.
choices.B: the mother of the boy who moved into the house.
choices.C: a neighbor recalling a time when the narrator was fourteen.
choices.D: an outside narrator who knows every character's thoughts.

candidates.explanation: The "I" is a neighbor recalling being fourteen, with no access to Mr. Halvorsen's thoughts.

A.rationale: Mr. Halvorsen never narrates or explains.

B.rationale: She is observed by the narrator; she does not narrate.

D.rationale: The narrator cannot know why Mr. Halvorsen planted the bulbs.

strategy.explanation: Identify the narrator and what the narrator can know.

candidates.remember: A first-person narrator cannot know other characters' thoughts.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, a male is likely to keep flying when a female's reply:

choices.A: comes after a delay that does not match his own species.
choices.B: is brighter than the flashes of females of his species.
choices.C: comes from a female perched on a leaf below him.
choices.D: is dimmer than the flashes the male himself produces.

candidates.evidence: A male who sees a flash at the wrong interval is likely to keep flying
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the timing matters as much as the flash, and a reply at the wrong interval tells the male it is not from his species.

B.rationale: Brightness is never mentioned as a signal.

C.rationale: Females of his own species also reply from leaves below.

D.rationale: The passage never says brightness determines whether a male lands.

hints: What does the passage say about the timing of the reply?

strategy.explanation: Find the sentence that begins "A male who sees."

candidates.remember: Detail answers restate a specific sentence.

revision_history.reason: solvers: an immediate reply is also a wrong interval, so old D was defensible; D replaced with a brightness distractor the passage does not support
